claims.claim: Keeping more than you need while others go without is a kind of theft.
Being rich is not wrong in itself; what matters is how you hold it and use it.
Money given to the poor honours God more than money spent making churches beautiful.

stances.summary: What you keep beyond your need was given you to manage, not to own. Refusing to clothe the naked when you could is no different from stripping them: you wrong everyone you could have helped.
stances.quote: The man who strips someone of his clothes will be called a thief. And the man who does not clothe the naked when he is able to, does he deserve any other name? The bread you are holding on to belongs to the hungry. The cloak you guard in your storerooms belongs to the naked.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 31) as reproduced at the url
stances.original: Ἢ ὁ μὲν ἐνδεδυμένον ἀπογυμνῶν λωποδύτης ὀνομασθήσεται· ὁ δὲ τὸν γυμνὸν μὴ ἐνδύων, δυνάμενος τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ἄλλης τινός ἐστι προσηγορίας ἄξιος; Τοῦ πεινῶντός ἐστιν ὁ ἄρτος, ὃν σὺ κατέχεις· τοῦ γυμνητεύοντος τὸ ἱμάτιον, ὃ σὺ φυλάσσεις ἐν ἀποθήκαις·
stances.work: Homily on the words "I will pull down my barns" (Luke 12:18), Homilia in illud: Destruam horrea mea
stances.context: Preached at Caesarea around 368, a famine year. Just before, Basil asks who the covetous man and the robber are, and answers that the man who makes his own what he received "for stewardship" (πρὸς οἰκονομίαν) is both. The sentence that follows closes the point: "So you wrong as many people as you could have helped." The popular English form of this line (bread in your cupboard, coat in your closet, money in the bank) is a modern paraphrase; Basil says the silver you have buried. No English translation before 1929 was found; the English versions in circulation are modern and copyrighted.

stances.summary: Not sharing is not a lesser fault than stealing: it is robbery of the poor. What the rich hold is not theirs but the poor's, because God gave the earth to all in common.
stances.quote: Not sharing our own goods with the poor is robbing the poor and taking away their life. What we hold on to is not ours, but theirs.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 48) as reproduced at the url
stances.original: τὸ μὴ μεταδιδόναι πένησιν ἐκ τῶν οἰκείων χρημάτων, ἁρπαγὴ πενήτων ἐστὶ καὶ ἀποστέρησις τῆς ἐκείνων ζωῆς· καὶ οὐ τὰ ἡμέτερα, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκείνων κατέχομεν.
stances.work: Second Sermon on Lazarus and the Rich Man (De Lazaro concio 2)
stances.context: Preached at Antioch in the late 380s. He asks the congregation, if they remember nothing else, to remember this one line. Earlier in the same sermon: "even this is robbery, not to share what one has" (καὶ γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο ἁρπαγὴ τὸ μὴ μεταδοῦναι τῶν ὄντων). The same view in public-domain English, Homily 12 on 1 Timothy (NPNF 1st series vol. 13, 1889; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230612.htm): "But is not this an evil, that you alone should have the Lord's property, that you alone should enjoy what is common?" The page at the url also carries a modern English translation by its blogger, which is copyrighted and was not used. The well-known English wording ("Not to share our own wealth with the poor is theft from the poor...") is Catharine Roth's 1984 translation, which is copyrighted.

stances.summary: When you give to the poor you are not being generous with your own; you are paying back what is theirs. The earth was given to all, and the rich have taken the common gift for themselves.
stances.quote: Not from your own do you bestow upon the poor man, but you make return from what is his. For what has been given as common for the use of all, you appropriate to yourself alone. The earth belongs to all, not to the rich
stances.translation: Martin R. P. McGuire, S. Ambrosii De Nabuthae (Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 15), Washington 1927
stances.original: non de tuo largiris pauperi, sed de suo reddis; quod enim commune est in omnium usum datum solus usurpas. omnium est terra, non diuitum
stances.context: Written around 389-395, closely modelled on Basil's sermons on wealth. The sentence continues: "Therefore you are paying a debt, you are not bestowing what is not due." The url is the archive.org OCR text of McGuire's 1927 edition (a US publication of 1927, public domain in the US since 2023); line breaks and spacing are OCR artefacts, and the OCR marks a footnote after "commune". Ambrose says the same in On the Duties of the Clergy 1.28.132 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34011.htm): "Nature, therefore, has produced a common right for all, but greed has made it a right for a few."

stances.summary: Keep what is enough for the life God gave you. Everything beyond that is other people's necessity, so the one who holds on to surplus is holding what belongs to others.
stances.quote: The superfluities of the rich are the necessaries of the poor. Thou possessest what belongs to others, when thou possessest more than thou needest.
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers, vol. 39 (Expositions on the Book of Psalms, vol. VI), Oxford 1857
stances.original: Superflua divitum, necessaria sunt pauperum. Res alienae possidentur, cum superflua possidentur.
stances.context: A sermon on almsgiving: "Find out how much He hath given thee, and take of that what is enough: all other things which remain as superfluities are the necessaries of others." The abridged NPNF version on New Advent cuts this passage out, so the 1857 Oxford translation is used (url is its archive.org OCR text; spacing is an OCR artefact). Latin checked at https://www.augustinus.it/latino/esposizioni_salmi/esposizione_salmo_205_testo.htm. He says the same in Sermon 61 (NPNF Sermon 11 on the New Testament, section 12): "Let your superfluities then be the poor man's necessaries." Augustine holds this together with a defence of the rich against the Pelagians (see claim b).

stances.summary: The earth is common to all. Those who keep God's common gift for private use are not innocent; giving the poor what they need is paying a debt of justice, not doing a favour.
stances.quote: For, when we administer necessaries of any kind to the indigent, we do not bestow our own, but render them what is theirs; we rather pay a debt of justice than accomplish works of mercy.
stances.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written around 590, addressed to those "who neither desire what belongs to others nor bestow what is their own." Just before: "Vainly, then, do those suppose themselves innocent, who claim to their own private use the common gift of God; ... since they almost daily slay so many persons as there are dying poor whose subsidies they keep close in their own possession." This is the book behind the site's planned Personality Quiz.

stances.person: The Sicilian Briton (anonymous Pelagian author of On Riches)
stances.summary: Some are poor because others hold more than they need. Take away the rich and there will be no poor: if no one owned more than necessary, everyone would have enough.
stances.quote: Others are in want because some possess more than they need. Take away the rich man and you will not find a poor one. Let no one possess more than is necessary, and everyone will have as much as is necessary.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin in C. P. Caspari, Briefe, Abhandlungen und Predigten (Christiania 1890), p. 48
stances.original: idcirco egere alios, quod alii superflua possideant. Tolle diuitem et pauperem non inuenies. Nemo plus, quam necessarium est, possideat, et, quantum necessarium est, omnes habebunt.
stances.context: HETERODOX: a Pelagian treatise written around 408-414, anonymous; often credited to the "Sicilian Briton", not securely to Pelagius himself. The next sentence: "For the few rich are the cause of the many poor" (Pauci enim diuites pauperum sunt causa multorum). The archive.org OCR misreads "pauperem" as "pauperera"; the other words match. The only English translation (B. R. Rees, 1991) is copyrighted.

stances.summary: God made all things for all, so their use is meant to be common. It is monstrous to live in luxury while many are in want, though Clement never calls owning property theft.
stances.quote: God brought our race into communion by first imparting what was His own, when He gave His own Word, common to all, and made all things for all. All things therefore are common, and not for the rich to appropriate an undue share.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, 1885
stances.location: Book 2, chapter 13 (ANF numbering), "Against excessive fondness for jewels and gold ornaments"
stances.context: A few lines later: "For God has given to us, I know well, the liberty of use, but only so far as necessary; and He has determined that the use should be common. And it is monstrous for one to live in luxury, while many are in want." The target is luxury, not ownership: in Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? 13-14 Clement defends keeping property so that one has something to give (see claim b).

stances.summary: God's gifts are common to all, like the sun and the rain. Sharing your harvest with others is simple justice and the way to imitate God the Father.
stances.quote: This is truly to become sons of God by spiritual birth; this is to imitate by the heavenly law the equity of God the Father. For whatever is of God is common in our use
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: On Works and Alms (De opere et eleemosynis)
stances.context: Written around 252-253, during plague. He praises the Jerusalem church that "had all things common" and ends: "he who, as a possessor in the earth, shares his returns and his fruits with the fraternity, while he is common and just in his gratuitous bounties, is an imitator of God the Father." He calls sharing just and godlike; he does not use the word theft. In section 13 he tells the hoarder: "You are the captive and slave of your money."

stances.summary: Rich and poor are later inventions of greed, backed by laws made by the strong. Look back to the equality God made at the start and help the poor out of your plenty.
stances.quote: Kinship was torn apart into the names of strangers, and greed carved up the nobility of nature, taking law as well to help its domination. But look, I beg you, to the first equality, not the later division; not to the law of the one who won the upper hand, but to the law of the One Who made us.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 35) as reproduced at the url
stances.original: ἐῤῥάγη τὸ συγγενὲς εἰς ὀνομάτων ἀλλοτριότητας, καὶ τὸ τῆς φύσεως εὐγενὲς πλεονεξία κατέτεμε, προσλαβοῦσα καὶ νόμον, τῆς δυναστείας ἐπίκουρον. Ἀλλὰ σὺ βλέπε μοι τὴν πρώτην ἰσονομίαν, μὴ τὴν τελευταίαν διαίρεσιν· μὴ τὸν τοῦ κρατήσαντος νόμον, ἀλλὰ τὸν τοῦ κτίσαντος.
stances.work: Oration 14, On Love of the Poor (De pauperum amore)
stances.context: Usually linked to Basil's poor-house at Caesarea in the early 370s; the date is debated. In section 25 he rebukes those who will not help "with their superfluities toward the necessities" of their kin, and says poverty and wealth "came in later" with sin. He frames surplus as a wrong against the original equality, but does not use the word theft. Not in NPNF (which omits Oration 14); no pre-1929 English translation was found.

stances.summary: Do not turn away anyone in need. Share everything with your brother and do not call it your own.
stances.quote: You shall not turn away from him that is in want, but you shall share all things with your brother, and shall not say that they are your own;
stances.translation: M. B. Riddle, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7, 1886
stances.work: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
stances.context: Anonymous, probably late first or early second century; not a person. The reason given: "for if you are partakers in that which is immortal, how much more in things which are mortal?" A rule of sharing, not an accusation of theft. Include only if the quiz allows anonymous texts.

stances.summary: God gave the earth in common, and failing to share one's surplus is part of how justice left the world. But private property is legitimate, and withholding is a lesser wrong than seizing.
stances.quote: For not only did they who had a superfluity fail to bestow a share upon others, but they even seized the property of others, drawing everything to their private gain;
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written around 303-311. In 5.5 he says that in the golden age "God had given the earth in common to all", but adds that this should not be taken to mean "that individuals at that time had no private property"; they simply shared. In 3.21-22 he rejects Plato's common ownership. So he treats hoarding surplus as injustice, while keeping it distinct from theft and defending ownership.

stances.summary: Money is only worth something when it is given away. Wealth piled up in one place leaves everyone else poorer.
stances.quote: Again, if all the money in the world were heaped up in one man's possession, all others would be made poor.
stances.translation: H. R. James, The Consolation of Philosophy, London 1897 (Project Gutenberg text)
stances.context: Written in prison around 524. Lady Philosophy speaks, and she is Boethius's voice. This is a philosopher's argument that riches are a poor sort of good because one person's heap is everyone else's lack. It is not a charge of theft or a duty to the poor. Also in Book 3, prose 8: "Is it thy endeavour to heap up money? Why, thou must wrest it from its present possessor!" A weak fit; use only if a softer voice is wanted.

stances.summary: Christ did not tell the rich to throw their money away but to rid their souls of the love of it. Wealth is a tool, blameless in itself; used well it serves righteousness, used badly it serves wrong.
stances.quote: Such an instrument is wealth. Are you able to make a right use of it? It is subservient to righteousness. Does one make a wrong use of it? It is, on the other hand, a minister of wrong. For its nature is to be subservient, not to rule.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (Quis dives salvetur)
stances.context: A whole treatise, written around 200, arguing this point. In section 11 he says Christ "does not, as some conceive off-hand, bid him throw away the substance he possessed". Section 13: "For if no one had anything, what room would be left among men for giving?" Section 14: "Riches, then, which benefit also our neighbours, are not to be thrown away." He still condemns luxury while others are in want (claim a).

stances.summary: Scripture condemns greed and pride, not gold or silver. Abraham was rich and is in heaven. The rich should stay humble, trust God and give freely.
stances.quote: In this Scripture it is covetousness that is condemned, not gold, or silver, or riches, but covetousness.
stances.translation: R. G. MacMullen, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 1st series, vol. 6, 1888
stances.work: Sermon 61 (Benedictine numbering; NPNF Sermon 11 on the New Testament)
stances.context: Just before: "It is one thing to be rich, another to wish to become rich." He argued the point at length against the Sicilian Pelagians in Letter 157 (around 414), sections 23-25, where he says the story of Lazarus shows "neither poverty honoured by God for its own sake in the one, nor riches condemned in the other" ("nec in isto paupertatem per seipsam divinitus honoratam, nec in illo divitias fuisse damnatas"; Latin at https://www.augustinus.it/latino/lettere/lettera_158_testo.htm, which is Letter 157 despite the file name; no pre-1929 English found). He also holds claim a: surplus belongs to the poor.

stances.summary: Equality does not come from taking away property but from taking away pride. Once the rich lose their arrogance and injustice, it makes no difference who is rich and who is poor.
stances.quote: For insolence and injustice being taken from the rich, it will make no difference whether some are rich and others poor, since they will be equal in spirit, and nothing but reverence towards God can produce this result.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Against Plato's common ownership. Just before: "He, therefore, who wishes to place men on an equality, ought not to take away marriage and wealth, but arrogance, pride, and haughtiness". He also blames greed for the loss of sharing (claim a, mixed).

stances.summary: Rich and poor need each other like the elm and the vine: the rich give, the poor pray for them. Wealth comes from the Lord so that it can be used for this service.
stances.quote: Blessed are they who have riches, and who understand that they are from the Lord.
stances.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Rome, early to mid second century. The whole parable of the elm and the vine makes the point. Similitude 1 adds: "Instead of lands, therefore, buy afflicted souls ... For to this end did the Master make you rich, that you might perform these services unto Him". The ANF text marks the words that follow as a doubtful addition.

stances.summary: Nearly everything Christians own came to them through a world of unjust gain. They are not to throw it away but to make it righteous by using it for the Lord and the poor.
stances.quote: For whatsoever we acquired from unrighteousness when we were heathen, we are proved righteous, when we have become believers, by applying it to the Lord's advantage.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Around 180, answering Marcionites who mocked the Israelites for taking Egyptian gold. He admits that Christians' houses and goods mostly come from "the mammon of unrighteousness", and mocks the critic who owns nothing and lives "naked, and barefoot ... among the mountains". Holding goods is defended, on condition that they are used well.

stances.summary: If God has made you rich, use your riches, but use them for salvation and for the poor. A large estate is a temptation unless it serves good ends.
stances.quote: Use them, certainly, but for the things of salvation; use them, but for good purposes; use them, but for those things which God has commanded, and which the Lord has set forth. Let the poor feel that you are wealthy; let the needy feel that you are rich.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: On the Dress of Virgins (De habitu virginum)
stances.context: Around 249, to wealthy consecrated virgins who said they should enjoy what God had given them. He grants that they may keep and use wealth, but not for display. Same section: "a large estate is a temptation, unless the wealth minister to good uses".

stances.summary: The guilt is not in possessions but in those who cannot use them. Riches block the wicked but help the good toward virtue, as Zacchaeus shows.
stances.quote: Let the rich learn that guilt attaches not to the goods themselves, but to those who know not how to use them. For riches, as they are hindrances to virtue in the unworthy, so are they means of advancing it in the good.
stances.translation: Catena Aurea on St Luke, ed. J. H. Newman, Oxford 1843 (English of Thomas Aquinas's excerpt)
stances.original: Discant non in facultatibus crimen haerere, sed in iis qui uti nesciant facultatibus; nam divitiae ut impedimenta in improbis, ita in bonis sunt adjumenta virtutis.
stances.work: Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke (Expositio evangelii secundum Lucam)
stances.context: Compiled from sermons and published around 389-390. The English comes through Aquinas's Catena, which adds "the rich" as the subject; Ambrose's Latin says simply "Let them learn". Latin checked at https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/Expositio_Evangelii_secundum_Lucam_(Ambrosius)/8, where the Migne column number 1493 is printed inside the sentence. Ambrose also holds claim a firmly (On Naboth), so for him "how you use it" means giving most of it away.

stances.summary: Job was very rich and very holy. He held his goods without delighting in them, so in intention he had already left them.
stances.quote: Nor had the power of that precept as yet shone out, which bids us leave all things; yet blessed Job already kept the intent of it in his heart, in that he surely had left his substance in intention, which he kept without taking delight in it.
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job, vol. 1, Oxford 1844
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Iob)
stances.context: Written around 579-595. Also Pastoral Rule 3.2: "the rich man may be humble and the poor man proud." Gregory holds claim a strongly as well (Pastoral Rule 3.21).

stances.summary: God may give riches, and much good is done with them; the woes fall on the faults that come with riches. Yet elsewhere he says the Lord always takes the side of the poor and condemns the rich in advance.
stances.quote: The endowing of a man indeed with riches, is not an incongruity to God, for by the help of riches even rich men are comforted and assisted; moreover, by them many a work of justice and charity is carried out. But yet there are serious faults which accompany riches;
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Against Marcion book 4 dates to about 207-208, when Tertullian was already drawn to the Montanist New Prophecy (HETERODOX by later judgement). He argues here that the God of the Old Testament also warns the rich, so the passage is partly polemical. In the earlier On Patience 7 (around 200-203; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0325.htm) he writes: "He always justifies the poor, fore-condemns the rich", and "nothing is ours, since all things are God's". Both are his own voice; the tone differs with the purpose.

stances.summary: Wealth, like wine, is not bad in itself; greed is. But he also says almost no fortune began without injustice, and that a rich man is good only when he gives his riches away.
stances.quote: Besides, he knew that wealth is not forbidden if it be used for that which is necessary. For as I observed, wine is not a bad thing, but drunkenness is so. A covetous man is one thing, and a rich man is another thing.
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 1st series, vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Antioch, 387. "He" is Paul in 1 Timothy 6:17. The other side of his view is in Homily 12 on 1 Timothy (NPNF 1st series vol. 13, 1889; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230612.htm): "So destructive a passion is avarice, that to grow rich without injustice is impossible", and "When he distributes his riches, he is good ... but while he keeps it himself, he is not good", ending "But if you are rich, you are no longer good." He is a deliberate middle voice: wealth is morally neutral as a thing, but keeping it is not.

stances.summary: All riches come from injustice: one person cannot gain unless another loses. The rich can still be saved, but it is hard, and selling everything is the perfect way.
stances.quote: He was right to say "of unrighteousness", for all riches come down from unrighteousness, and unless one person loses, another cannot find. So that common saying seems to me most true: a rich man is either unrighteous or the heir of an unrighteous man.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne, PL 22) as reproduced at the url
stances.original: Pulchre dixit de iniquo; omnes enim divitiae de iniquitate descendunt, et nisi alter perdiderit, alter non potest invenire. Unde et illa vulgata sententia mihi videtur esse verissima. Dives autem iniquus, aut iniqui haeres.
stances.context: Around 407, explaining "make friends of the mammon of unrighteousness" (Luke 16:9) to a rich widow. The saying is a proverb he adopts, not his coinage; this text prints "autem" where other editions read "aut". He goes straight on: "Not impossible, but difficult". In Letter 130.14 (to Demetrias, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6) selling all is "the climax of complete and apostolic virtue" but "full freedom of choice is left to every individual". Letter 58.2 (to Paulinus of Nola) scorns Christians "who cram our pockets with gold and cling under pretext of almsgiving to our old riches". Letter 120 is not in NPNF; no pre-1929 English found.

stances.summary: Whoever loves his neighbour as himself owns no more than his neighbour. So great wealth is itself the evidence of too little love.
stances.quote: So the one who loves his neighbour as himself owns nothing more than his neighbour. Yet you are plainly a man of many possessions. Where did they come from? Clearly from putting your own enjoyment ahead of relief for the many. So the more you abound in wealth, the more you fall short in love.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 31:281) as reproduced at the url
stances.original: Ὥστε ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν πλησίον ὡς ἑαυτὸν οὐδὲν περισσότερον κέκτηται τοῦ πλησίον· ἀλλὰ μὴν φαίνῃ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά. Πόθεν ταῦτα; ἢ δῆλον ὅτι τὴν οἰκείαν ἀπόλαυσιν προτι μοτέραν τῆς τῶν πολλῶν παραμυθίας ποιούμενος. Ὅσον οὖν πλεονάζεις τῷ πλούτῳ, τοσοῦτον ἐλλείπεις τῇ ἀγάπῃ.
stances.work: Homily to the Rich (Homilia in divites)
stances.context: Preached at Caesarea around 368, on the rich young man. The Greek page prints "προτι μοτέραν" split in two; it is one word. Basil does allow that wealth is received "for stewardship" (Homily 6.7), so his objection is to staying rich while others lack, not to ever handling money. He holds claim a strongly.

stances.person: The Sicilian Briton (anonymous Pelagian author of On Riches)
stances.summary: Riches cannot be separated from greed. Almost every fortune is made through wrong, and anyone who truly stops being greedy gives his surplus away and so stops being rich.
stances.quote: He is not greedy who gives generously to the needy from what he has. Whoever has begun to give his goods away generously will soon have nothing left over, and whoever has nothing left over can no longer be rich, since a rich man is reckoned by the excess of what he owns. So as soon as anyone stops being greedy, he also stops being rich.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin in C. P. Caspari, Briefe, Abhandlungen und Predigten (Christiania 1890), p. 26
stances.original: Auarus enim ille non est, qui ex his, quae habet, indigentibus largius praerogat; et qui sua largius praerogare iam coeperit, nihil incipiet habere superfluum; et qui superfluum nihil habuerit, nec diues esse iam poterit, quia diues ex superflua possidendi nimietate censetur. Itaque ut quisque auarus esse desinit, esse cessat et diues.
stances.context: HETERODOX: Pelagian, around 408-414. The treatise's thesis is that the rich cannot enter the kingdom unless they give up their riches; Augustine answered this teaching in Letter 157. In chapter 8 the author asks what the chief origin of riches is "if not injustice and plunder" (iniquitas et rapina). The OCR at the url has small misreadings ("bis" for his, "Inrgius" for largius, "nee" for nec).

stances.summary: Honour Christ in the poor before you honour Him with gold cups. God needs golden souls, not golden vessels, and your hungry brother is more truly His temple than the building.
stances.quote: Even so do thou honor Him with this honor, which He ordained, spending your wealth on poor people. Since God has no need at all of golden vessels, but of golden souls.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 1st series, vol. 10, 1888
stances.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
stances.context: Antioch, around 390. In the same section: "Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked". Then: "Do not therefore while adorning His house overlook your brother in distress, for he is more properly a temple than the other." He adds that he says this "not forbidding munificence in these matters, but admonishing you to do those other works together with these, or rather even before these." In Homily 80.2 on Matthew: if someone asks before giving vessels to a church, "command it to be given to the poor", but if the gift is already made, do not undo it.

stances.summary: The real temple of Christ is the believer's soul, and Christ is hungry in the poor. Jewelled walls are worth nothing beside that, though he will not blame those who build churches.
stances.quote: The true temple of Christ is the believer's soul; adorn this, clothe it, offer gifts to it, welcome Christ in it.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Around 395. The next sentence: "What use are walls blazing with jewels when Christ in His poor is in danger of perishing from hunger?" (New Advent prints a Scripture reference inside that sentence). Letter 52.10: "Many build churches nowadays; their walls and pillars of glowing marble ... Yet to the choice of Christ's ministers no heed is paid"; "our Lord by His poverty has consecrated the poverty of His house." Letter 125.20 praises Bishop Exuperius of Toulouse, who gave all to the poor and carried the Lord's body "in a wicker basket" and the blood in "his plain glass-cup". Qualification, Letter 130.14: "Others may build churches ... I do not blame those who do these things ... However your duty is of a different kind. It is yours to clothe Christ in the poor". Paulinus, the recipient, later built richly decorated churches at Nola.

stances.summary: He broke up the church's sacred vessels to ransom captives and defended it: the Church keeps gold to spend on the needy, and living people are better vessels than gold ones.
stances.quote: The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out, and to spend on those who need. What necessity is there to guard what is of no good?
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis ministrorum)
stances.context: Around 388-391, defending his own act after the Gothic raids of 378, which "could displease the Arians". Same section: "It had been better to preserve living vessels than gold ones." Section 140 tells how the martyr Lawrence pointed to the poor: "These are the treasures of the Church." Qualification, section 142: vessels may be sold for the poor, for captives, for burial ground, and also because "a temple of the Lord is built"; consecrated chalices are to be kept back unless nothing else is left (143).

stances.summary: God does not eat or drink or need cups, so the church's gold and silver vessels should be sold to ransom and feed starving prisoners, even enemy prisoners.
stances.quote: Our God, my brethren, needs neither dishes nor cups; for he neither eats nor drinks, nor is in want of anything.
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 2, 1890
stances.context: Bishop of Amida in Mesopotamia, around 420-422. His words are reported by the historian Socrates about twenty years later, so near-contemporary but not his own writing. He melted the vessels to ransom about seven thousand Persian captives and sent them home. The NPNF prints "he" in lower case for God; the site's capitals rule would show "He".

stances.summary: When church funds ran out he had the sacred vessels melted down for captives and the poor. He never wanted new buildings, though he did not stop others who built without extravagance.
stances.quote: For the sake of captives and of the many who were in need he even ordered the holy vessels to be broken and melted down and to be distributed to the needy. I would not have mentioned this unless I knew that it was done contrary to the carnal judgment of some.
stances.translation: Herbert T. Weiskotten, Sancti Augustini Vita scripta a Possidio episcopo, Princeton 1919
stances.context: Possidius lived with Augustine for nearly forty years and wrote soon after his death in 430. This records Augustine's acts, not his words. Just before: "For new buildings he never had any desire ... Nevertheless he did not restrain those who desired or constructed them, provided only they were not extravagant." Possidius cites Ambrose as precedent. The "carnal judgment of some" shows that people objected.

stances.summary: Selling a church's consecrated vessels is normally wrong and punishable. It is allowed, with proper witnesses, when the purpose is mercy, such as ransoming captives.
stances.quote: As it is reprehensible and deserving of punishment for any one to sell consecrated vessels except in cases sanctioned by law and the sacred canons, so it is not a matter for reproach or penalty if they should be disposed of with a compassionate purpose for the redemption of captives.
stances.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 12, 1895
stances.location: Book 7, Letter 13, to Fortunatus of Fano
stances.context: Around 597. A careful middle position: church treasure is protected by law, but captives come first. He requires the sale to be witnessed to avoid scandal. He holds claim a strongly (Pastoral Rule 3.21).

stances.summary: A splendid church, built with generous spending, is a fitting honour to God and a visible image of the spiritual temple.
stances.quote: But the royal house he has furnished with more beautiful and splendid materials, using unstinted liberality in his disbursements.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Church History, Panegyric on the building of the churches (to Paulinus of Tyre)
stances.context: Around 315, at the dedication of the rebuilt church at Tyre after the persecution. He praises the lavish building and calls it "this magnificent temple of the highest God, corresponding to the pattern of the greater as a visible to an invisible" (10.4.26). He never weighs it against giving to the poor, so he disagrees only by implication. No early Christian was found arguing directly that money for church beauty honours God more than alms.

splits_fathers: Claim a is close to one-sided among the Fathers. Basil, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine and Gregory the Great all say in plain words that surplus kept back belongs to the poor, and the Pelagian On Riches goes furthest of all. Clement, Cyprian, Gregory of Nazianzus and the Didache lean the same way in softer terms. No early Christian was found defending the keeping of surplus as innocent. The only brakes are Lactantius, who defends private property against Plato and treats withholding as a lesser wrong than seizing, and Clement, who condemns luxury but not ownership. Claim b is where the real disagreement lies, with strong voices on both sides. Clement (a whole treatise), Augustine (against the Pelagians), Lactantius and Hermas say wealth is a neutral tool; Irenaeus, Cyprian, Ambrose and Gregory the Great agree more briefly. Against them, Basil says great wealth proves a lack of love, Jerome adopts the proverb that every rich man is unjust or the heir of one, and the Pelagian On Riches says a man who stops being greedy stops being rich. Chrysostom and Tertullian stand in the middle. Most Fathers held a and b together: wealth is not evil in itself, but the right use of it is to give most of it away. Claim c is mostly agreed. Chrysostom, Jerome and Ambrose say it outright, Acacius and Augustine acted on it, and Gregory the Great allowed it under rules. But nearly all of them refused to condemn church building: Chrysostom does not forbid gifts, Jerome does not blame builders, Ambrose lists building a church as a proper use of church gold, and Augustine let others build if they were not extravagant. The other side appears only as praise of splendid churches (Eusebius at Tyre) and as unnamed objectors (the Arians who blamed Ambrose, the 'carnal judgment of some' in Possidius). No early Christian was found arguing that church beauty honours God more than alms.
splits_people_today: Claim a splits people sharply and is a good question for the quiz. Many Christians, especially in the United States and in free-market traditions, see giving as voluntary charity and would reject the word theft. Catholic social teaching quotes Chrysostom and Gregory the Great on this point in the Catechism (2446), and many Orthodox, progressive Protestants and secular egalitarians would agree. Claim b is close to one-sided today: most people, religious or not, would agree that being rich is fine if you are generous. Only a minority (radical Christians, some ascetics, some on the anti-capitalist left) would disagree. So a disagree answer tells the quiz a lot, while an agree answer tells it little unless the statement is sharpened (for example, 'You can stay rich and still be a good Christian, as long as you give generously'). Claim c splits people on tradition and taste. Many evangelicals, low-church Protestants and secular people would agree that the poor come first. Many Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans who value beauty in worship would disagree or hesitate, often citing John 12 (Judas objecting to the costly ointment). Among the Fathers it is much less split than among people today.

misattributions.line: The bread in your cupboard belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the naked; the shoes you do not wear belong to the barefoot; the money in your bank belongs to the poor.
misattributions.attributed_to: often Ambrose or John Chrysostom; sometimes Basil
misattributions.truth: Basil the Great, Homily on 'I will pull down my barns' (Homily 6), section 7. The core is genuine, but 'cupboard', 'closet' and 'bank' are modern paraphrase: Basil speaks of bread you hold, a cloak in your storerooms, a shoe rotting beside you and silver you have buried.

misattributions.line: Every rich man is a thief, or the heir of a thief.
misattributions.truth: Not in Chrysostom in this form. Homily 12 on 1 Timothy argues that an inherited fortune almost certainly began in injustice, but without the proverb. The proverb is quoted by Jerome (Letter 120.1, and his short notes on the Psalms) as a common or 'philosopher's' saying: 'a rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man'. It is not Jerome's coinage either.

misattributions.line: Take away the rich and you will find no poor (Tolle divitem et pauperem non invenies).
misattributions.truth: From the anonymous Pelagian treatise On Riches (De divitiis) 12.2, around 408-414, usually credited to the 'Sicilian Briton'. It is not securely by Pelagius himself.

misattributions.line: Not to share our own wealth with the poor is theft from the poor and deprivation of their means of life; we do not possess our own wealth but theirs.
misattributions.truth: Genuine: Second Sermon on Lazarus, near the end. The wording is Catharine Roth's 1984 translation (copyrighted), so it cannot be reproduced as is; the rendering in this file is made from the Greek.

notes: 1. Do not set a against b. Most Fathers hold both: wealth is a tool, and the right use of the tool is to give the surplus away (Clement, Augustine, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Gregory the Great). The real divide on b is between 'wealth is neutral' (Clement, Augustine, Lactantius, Hermas) and 'being rich itself shows a failure of love or justice' (Basil's Homily to the Rich, Jerome's Letter 120, the Pelagian On Riches). A sharper b statement would separate them better, for example 'You can stay rich and still be a good Christian, as long as you give generously.' 2. Best pairings for 'nearest and farthest': Clement against the Pelagian On Riches (and against Basil) on b; Chrysostom and Jerome against Eusebius on c, with the caution that Eusebius disagrees only by implication. 3. Capitals: several public-domain quotations print pronouns for God in lower case (Acacius in Socrates, 'he neither eats nor drinks'). The owner's rule is capitals inside quotations too; the machine check must run on the page text, and the display can then apply the rule. 4. Own renderings: Basil (Homilies 6 and 7), Chrysostom (Lazarus 2), Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 14), Jerome (Letter 120) and the Pelagian On Riches have no English before 1929 that could be found, so the English in this file is a close rendering of the original text at the url; check the 'original' field against the page. 5. Leads that did not hold or were left out: Origen's Commentary on Matthew 15.14 quotes the Gospel of the Hebrews (Christ telling the rich man his brothers are 'dying of hunger' while his house is full); the words are the apocryphal gospel's, surviving only in the Latin version, so they are not Origen's position. Life of Antony 2-3 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 4) tells how Antony gave his 300 acres to the villagers and his goods to the poor on hearing 'sell what you have'; Athanasius presents it as Antony's own call, not a rule for everyone, so it is not recorded as a stance. Tertullian's Apology 39 ('All things are common among us but our wives') describes sharing in the church, not a theft claim. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43.63 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 7), sets Basil's poor-house above the wonders of the world and 'shrines that are no more', but those are pagan monuments, not churches. Gregory of Nyssa's sermons on the love of the poor could not be found in Greek online, and their English is modern, so Nyssa is not recorded. No verified words of Paulinus of Nola on c were found; he gave away a great fortune yet built richly decorated churches at Nola, and Jerome's Letter 58 (quoted under c) was written to him. 6. The strongest single lines for a reveal: Basil's 'The bread you are holding on to belongs to the hungry' (a); Chrysostom's 'What we hold on to is not ours, but theirs' (a); Clement's 'Such an instrument is wealth' (b); Basil's 'the more you abound in wealth, the more you fall short in love' (b); Chrysostom's 'God has no need at all of golden vessels, but of golden souls' (c); Ambrose's 'The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out' (c).
